Stated Claim / Post Context:
Beau Lamarre-Condon's friend tells jury: He told me we were going to farm because 'he had to save the cattle', not to dump bodies

Follow Daily Mail's live coverage of Beau Lamarre-Condon's murder trial.

Actual Article Body:
By CHARLOTTE KARP, SENIOR NEWS REPORTER

Updated:  11:08 AEDT, 23 October 2026

Former cop Beau Lamarre-Condon allegedly told his female friend they were going to a rural farm to stop cattle from escaping when they were actually there to dump the bodies of Jesse Baird and Luke Davies.

Lamarre-Condon's childhood friend, known by the pseudonym Elizabeth Kennedy for legal reasons, told the NSW Supreme Court earlier this week that she agreed to the road trip on February 21, 2024, but didn't realise how far they would go.

Ms Kennedy said she thought they were going to book accommodation for their planned Europe trip, and was 'annoyed' when she realised they were driving about 200km away from Sydney to Bungonia, near Goulburn.

She told the court Lamarre-Condon explained he had to break into a farm, which belonged to an 'old family friend', because 'the cattle were going to break out'.

'He had to break in and save the cattle,' she said.

The court previously heard the Bungonia property actually belonged to the family of a man Lamarre-Condon met on Hinge in 2023. He had visited the property once before, during an overnight date.

Once they arrived at the farm, Ms Kennedy told the court she saw Lamarre-Condon cut the lock on the front gate before driving into the property and leaving her alone for about 40 minutes.

Lamarre-Condon is accused of fatally shooting Baird and Davies in Paddington on February 19, 2024, before bundling their bodies into a white Toyota HiAce rental van, and driving them to Cella Farm in Bungonia on February 21.

Pictured: Beau Lamarre-Condon with Elizabeth Kennedy in Bunnings, Goulburn

He allegedly tried to sink the bodies in a dam, before dragging them to a fence line and covering them with rocks and tree foliage.

Lamarre-Condon claims it was Ms Kennedy's idea to hide the bodies, but she told the court she was left alone at the property gate and had no idea there were bodies in the car throughout their road trip.

He has pleaded not guilty to two counts of domestic violence-related murder and one count of break and enter.

Follow Daily Mail's live coverage of Beau Lamarre-Condon's murder trial below.

A judge has told Beau Lamarre-Condon's male friend that he will not be charged over his part in the alleged double murder.

The friend, who cannot be identified for legal reasons, gave evidence over AVL on Friday morning.

Crown prosecutors asked if he was willing to give evidence about his time with Lamarre-Condon after the alleged murders.

Justice Natalie Adams said his evidence may prove that he concealed a serious offence.

He was granted a certificate, which means he can't be charged with any offences based on his evidence unless he lies on the stand.

The court was not in session on Thursday.

The matter resumed at 10am on Friday with a scheduled legal argument.

Coverage will resume when the legal argument concludes.

On Wednesday, Beau Lamarre-Condon's childhood friend, known as Elizabeth Kennedy for legal reasons, concluded her evidence.

Ms Kennedy (pictured below, with Lamarre-Condon) told the court that he drove her from Sydney to Goulburn on February 21, 2024 - two days after he allegedly killed Jesse Baird and Luke Davies.

She said that she had no idea they were going to Goulburn and was 'annoyed' when she realised they were driving two hours away from Sydney.

Ms Kennedy told the court Lamarre-Condon asked her to turn her phone off. He also had his iPhone switched off, but was using the map on an Android phone.

When Crown prosecutors asked if she could see the location on the map, Ms Kennedy said: 'I can't read a map, I don't drive, and I've never had a licence.'

She told the court that Lamarre-Condon barely spoke about Baird during the trip, which she said was strange.

'He said, "Guess what? Jesse's seeing someone new",' she recalled.

'I could tell he was upset, but he was still very bubbly and very talkative, so I didn't think it affected him that much.'

She said it was 'odd' because the conversation would normally revolve entirely around Baird.

Once they arrived at Cella Farm in Bungonia, she saw him cut the lock at the front gate and asked her to cover the rental van number plate with a garbage bag.

Ms Kennedy said he then went around the back of the property, where she couldn't see him anymore, and left her at the gate for about 40 minutes.

When Ms Kennedy was alone, she started panicking.

'I was hyperventilating and crying,' she told the court.

'I had a panic attack, I was squatting, I wanted to turn my phone on ... He came back and told me to shush because I was panicking and he asked if I'd called anyone and I said no.'

'He said, "I'm going to take you home right now", and I started to calm down.'

Ms Kennedy said it was an 'awful' drive home because she had been panicking and the air conditioning was freezing.

'He told me not to speak, even though I was freezing cold. He let me turn my air vent off but I wasn't allowed to close the windows,' she said.

She told the court Lamarre-Condon asked about her anxiety medication and if she'd 'thought about ending it all'.

The following day, Ms Kennedy tried to call Beau Lamarre-Condon about 12 times when she saw news reports of Baird's disappearance.

Eventually, he called her on the encrypted messaging app Signal.

She told the court: 'I saw the news the night before that Jesse was missing and I had some questions.

'He said he couldn't answer them on the phone, he said he was seeing police on Friday morning because he had a meeting with them.'

During the call, the court heard Ms Kennedy said to Lamarre-Condon: 'Have you seen the news?'

The court heard he replied: 'Yeah, it's crazy. I have to go to Bondi Police Station to talk to detectives tomorrow.'

She asked: 'Do you know where Jesse is?'

He replied: 'No, it's just crazy.'

The pair had planned to go to Europe together later that year. On the call, Lamarre-Condon allegedly said: 'If I can't go to Europe with you, I'm so sorry, I love you.'

She said, 'It felt like a final call ... He sounded apologetic, a bit stressed, and then he hung up and tried to call him back after that but the phone was off.'

Ms Kennedy said she told her partner about the situation that evening and they decided to talk to a lawyer.

She went to Bondi Police Station the following day, made a statement and drove with detectives to Goulburn to find the Bungonia farm.

During cross-examination by defence lawyer John Stratton SC, Ms Kennedy told the court the only thing she could smell in the van was air freshener.

'To be fair, I don't know what a dead body smells like,' she said.

Mr Stratton asked her if she could see into the back of the van.

She said the back area of the van was obscured by a mesh cage, which meant she could only see a blue tarp that appeared to be flat on the floor.

He asked: 'Did it look like there were two dead bodies under it?'

Ms Kennedy replied: 'That was the last thing I was thinking.'

He said: 'It didn't look to you like the tarp was hiding a wheelbarrow, a spade or bags of cement?'

She said: 'No.'

He asked: 'Did [Lamarre-Condon] say to you, "Hey, before you get in the van, I need you to know it's serious and I'm not joking, if you don't want to help, I understand".'

Ms Kennedy replied: 'No, he never mentioned anything about helping him with anything.'

Mr Stratton asked: 'Did [Lamarre-Condon] lift the tarp and show you the head of a deceased Jesse Baird?'

She replied: 'No, he definitely didn't want me to know there was anything in the back.'

He asked: 'Did you say, "Oh my God, I saw his head, you weren't joking"?'

Ms Kennedy said that never happened. She also denied that Lamarre-Condon started crying.

She told the court: 'He never showed any remorse or shed a tear, even when he called me from jail.'

Mr Stratton asked Ms Kennedy if she convinced him to hide the bodies rather than go to the police.

He asked her: 'Did you say, "No, no, no, you can't go to the police, they won't believe you, this is like the Taylor Swift song, No Body, No Crime"?'

Ms Kennedy denied saying anything like that.

She told the court Lamarre-Condon played the song during their trip to Goulburn: 'It's a really niche song ... I tried to play a few more songs from that album and he didn't know any of them.'
